extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's Foundations/The Rising Sea)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, constructions, and key properties/criteria for globally generated sheaves, base-point-free line bundles, the relationship between graded modules and quasicoherent sheaves on Proj, and the pushforward/pullback functors for quasicoherent sheaves (including their adjointness and exactness properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Globally generated at a point
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasicoherent sheaf F is globally generated at p if every germ at p is a linear combination (over the local ring O_{X,p}) of germs of global sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, surjectivity of the map from the space of global sections (tensor O_{X,p}?) to the stalk can be checked on stalks; one can take a single index set for all of X by union over points. See Exercises and following remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Globally generated (global notion)
rubrics_metrics.description: F is globally generated if it is globally generated at every point p ∈ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the stalkwise criterion (surjectivity on stalks) to check this. For finite type qc sheaves on quasicompact schemes, generation at closed points can imply global generation (see 15.3.C(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine schemes: global generation of quasicoherent sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Every quasicoherent sheaf on every affine scheme is globally generated; every finite type quasicoherent sheaf on an affine scheme is generated by a finite number of global sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: For any A-module M there is a surjection from a free A-module onto M. (Exercise 15.3.A.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability under direct sums and tensor products
rubrics_metrics.description: If F and G are globally generated (or finitely globally generated, or generated at a point p), then F ⊕ G and F ⊗ G are also globally generated (with the analogous finite/fiberwise variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 15.3.B states these closure properties explicitly; similar statements hold for invertible sheaves (tensor of two base-point-free line bundles is base-point-free).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiber criterion for global generation at a point
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite type quasicoherent sheaf F, F is globally generated at p iff the map from global sections to the fiber F_p / m_p F_p is surjective (m_p the maximal ideal of O_{X,p}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Geometric Nakayama (Exercise 13.7.E). (Exercise 15.3.C(a).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Local openness of generation
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is globally generated at p (finite type qc sheaf), then there exists an open neighborhood U of p on which F is globally generated at every point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Exercise 15.3.C(b): global generation at a point implies generation on some neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed-point criterion on quasicompact schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is quasicompact and F a finite type quasicoherent sheaf, then if F is globally generated at all closed points of X, it is globally generated at all points of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses existence of closed points in nonempty quasicompact schemes (Exercise 5.1.E). (Exercise 15.3.C(c).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite generation equivalence on quasicompact schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a finite type quasicoherent sheaf on a quasicompact scheme X, then F is globally generated iff it is generated by a finite number of global sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 15.3.D; ties the stalkwise/global notions to finite generating sets when X is quasicompact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invertible sheaf global generation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: An invertible sheaf L on X is globally generated iff for every point p ∈ X there exists a global section of L not vanishing at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently L is base-point-free. See Exercise 15.3.E and Theorem 16.4.1 for importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base points and base locus (definition and properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an invertible sheaf L, points where all global sections vanish are base points; their set is the base locus, a closed subset. The complement is the base-point-free locus; L is base-point-free iff it has no base points (equivalently globally generated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can refine to a scheme-theoretic base locus (intersection of vanishing loci of sections). Tensoring base-point-free line bundles preserves being base-point-free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map to projective space from sections of a line bundle
rubrics_metrics.description: Given s_0,...,s_n global sections of an invertible sheaf L on X with no common zero, they define a morphism X → P^n (locally by trivializing L and applying exercise 6.3.M(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: on open sets where L is trivial, interpret the s_i as functions and use the map to P^n; show these local maps agree on overlaps (Exercise 15.3.F). This yields maps to projective space over Z or any base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear series (definition and base-point notions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear series on a k-scheme X is a k-vector space V, an invertible sheaf L, and a linear map λ: V → Γ(X,L). If λ is an isomorphism it's the complete linear series |L|. A point where all elements of V vanish is a base point of the linear series; if none exist the series is base-point-free and defines a morphism to projective space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate base locus and scheme-theoretic base locus notions to linear series. An (n+1)-dimensional base-point-free linear series defines a morphism to P^n_k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's Theorem A (finite generation of twists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose S is a finitely generated graded algebra generated in degree 1 over A = S_0. For any finite type quasicoherent sheaf F on Proj S, there exists n_0 such that for all n ≥ n_0, F(n) is finitely globally generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as Theorem 15.3.8; it is a key global generation result for twists on projective schemes and will be a consequence of Theorem 16.6.2. Use it to obtain surjections from sums of O onto twists and then untwist by tensoring (as in the proof sketch of 15.3.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between graded modules and quasicoherent sheaves on Proj (Γ and ~ functors)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a graded S-module M and a quasicoherent sheaf F on Proj S, define Γ_n(F) := Γ(Proj S, F(n)); Γ(F) is a graded S-module. There is a saturation functor M ↦ M^# and a natural 'saturation map' M → Γ(~M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 15.4.A–15.4.F develop these constructions. The saturation behaves like sheafification; M ↦ ~M and Γ are adjoint up to saturation. The saturation map need not be injective/surjective in general (Exercise 15.4.D), but under finiteness hypotheses it is an isomorphism in high degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every quasicoherent sheaf on a projective A-scheme arises from a graded module
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 15.4.3: every quasicoherent sheaf on a projective A-scheme comes from the ~ construction applied to some graded module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Γ and saturation constructions; this justifies studying quasicoherent sheaves on Proj via graded modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subschemes of Proj correspond to homogeneous ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Each closed subscheme Z ⊂ Proj S arises from a homogeneous ideal I ⊂ S (Exercise 15.4.H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses left-exactness of ~ and the Γ functor; this is the projective analogue of closed subschemes of affine schemes being cut out by ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjointness of Γ and ~ (saturation/adjonction)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural bijection Hom(~M, F) ≅ Hom(M, Γ(F)) describing Γ and ~ as adjoint functors (Exercise 15.4.I), interpreted via compatible local maps over D(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the bijection explicit by describing compatible maps on ((M~)_f)_0 and ((Γ(F))_f)_0 as f varies through S_+.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturation as 'best' graded module
rubrics_metrics.description: Saturated graded S-modules are the 'best' representatives giving a quasicoherent sheaf on Proj; different graded modules can give same sheaf but saturation picks canonical one. There is a bijection between saturated qc sheaves of ideals and closed subschemes of Proj S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 15.4.5 discussion: saturation is analogous to sheafification and is idempotent (saturation of saturation equals saturation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushforward under affine morphism preserves quasicoherence and is exact
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is an affine morphism then π_* sends QCoh_X to QCoh_Y and π_* is an exact functor QCoh_X → QCoh_Y (Exercises 16.2.A and 16.2.B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On affines this corresponds to the familiar module pushforward/restriction-of-scalars construction; use this to deduce properties in the affine case and glue for more general statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushforward of a quasicoherent sheaf is quasicoherent under quasicompact quasiseparated morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 16.2.1: If π: X → Y is quasicompact and quasiseparated and F is quasicoherent on X, then π_* F is quasicoherent on Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes the affine-case result; the quasicompact/quasiseparated hypotheses are used to ensure the image is quasicoherent (see Exercise 13.3.F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence need not be preserved by pushforward in general
rubrics_metrics.description: Coherent sheaves do not always push forward to coherent sheaves (example: structure morphism π: A^1_k → Spec k gives π_* O_{A^1_k} corresponding to k[t], not finite over k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, under favorable hypotheses (finite morphism between locally Noetherian schemes, projective/proper morphisms with Noetherian hypotheses) pushforwards of coherent sheaves are coherent (Exercise 16.2.C, Theorem 18.8.1(d), Grothendieck Coherence Theorem 18.9.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three equivalent constructions/ways to think of pullback
rubrics_metrics.description: Pullback π^*G can be understood (a) module-theoretically on affines by Γ(Spec A, π^*G) = N ⊗_B A when G|_{Spec B} corresponds to N, (b) by the universal property Hom_{O_X}(π^*G, F) ≅ Hom_{O_Y}(G, π_*F), and (c) by the explicit ringed-space formula π^*G := π^{-1}G ⊗_{π^{-1}O_Y} O_X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each perspective has advantages: (a) is concrete for proofs with affines, (b) is conceptual (adjointness), (c) is short and works on ringed spaces; combine them to conclude π^* preserves quasicoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of pullback as adjoint and its compatibility with restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: If π^* satisfies the universal property then restriction behaves well: (π^* G)|_{π^{-1}(V)} ≅ (π|_{π^{-1}(V)})^*(G|_V). Pullback exists (at least in Mod_{O_Y}) via the explicit construction and respects quasicoherence when π is a morphism of schemes (Exercises 16.3.A–D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important for gluing local affine constructions to obtain the global pullback of quasicoherent sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjunction of pushforward and pullback for quasicompact quasiseparated morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 16.3.6: If π: X → Y is quasicompact and quasiseparated, π_* and π^* form an adjoint pair on QCoh: Hom_{O_X}(π^*G, F) ≅ Hom_{O_Y}(G, π_*F), functorial in F∈QCoh_X and G∈QCoh_Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses ensure π_* indeed maps QCoh_X to QCoh_Y (use Theorem 16.2.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Key properties of pullback (Theorem 16.3.7 list)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π: X → Y and quasicoherent G on Y, the pullback π^* satisfies: (1) π^* O_Y ≅ O_X; (2) preserves finite type quasicoherent sheaves (hence preserves coherence under Noetherian hypotheses); (3) preserves locally free sheaves and their transition matrices; (4) functoriality in morphisms (composition law for pullbacks); (5) functoriality in the sheaf (π^* is a functor QCoh_Y → QCoh_X); (6) pulls back sections (s ↦ π^*s) and their vanishing loci; (7) stalk formula (π^*G)_p ≅ G_q ⊗_{O_{Y,q}} O_{X,p} for π(p)=q; (8) fiber formula on residue fields; (9) π^*(G ⊗ G') ≅ π^*G ⊗ π^*G'; (10) π^* is right-exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are interrelated and many are proved via the affine/tensor-product description; right-exactness follows from tensor product right-exactness. Use these to compute local behavior, to check vector bundle pullbacks, and to deduce flatness notion when π^* is exact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness criterion (remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π: X → Y is flat iff the functor π^* from QCoh_Y to QCoh_X is exact (not merely right-exact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a central notion developed further in Chapter 24; flatness ensures exactness of pulling back sequences of sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety pulling back ideal sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: If i: X ↪ Y is a closed embedding and µ: Y' → Y any morphism, for the pullback square X' = X ×_Y Y' the canonical map µ^*(I_{X/Y}) → I_{X'/Y'} need not be an isomorphism in general; µ^*(I_{X/Y}) maps onto I_{X'/Y'} and equality holds under flatness assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: applying µ^* to the closed-embedding exact sequence yields only right-exactness in general; afﬁne-locally the ideal of the pullback is generated by pullbacks of generators (Exercise 16.3.F). If µ is flat then µ^*I_{X/Y} ≅ I_{X'/Y'}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of morphisms to projective space via line bundles and sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 16.4.1: For fixed X, morphisms X → P^n are in bijection with data (L, s_0,...,s_n) where L is an invertible sheaf and the s_i are sections with no common zeros, modulo isomorphism of the data (multiplying by units in O_X gives the same map).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the coordinate-free description: maps to P^n correspond to n+1 sections of a line bundle not vanishing simultaneously, modulo automorphisms coming from O_X^*. This generalizes to maps to projective schemes via sections satisfying relations (example given for a curve in P^2).
